one_liner: Single-file embeddable Scheme interpreter (s7.c + s7.h); ran recursive fib(34) about 4.5x faster than Duktape 1.2.2 in Scriptorium 2015.
what_it_does: s7 is Bill Schottstaedt's Scheme interpreter for CCRMA's Snd, built to be an extension language: you compile s7.c into your program, call s7_init to get an s7_scheme instance, then s7_eval_c_string, s7_load or s7_call, and expose C functions with s7_define_function / s7_define_safe_function and new types with s7_make_c_type. It is close to Guile 1.8 as a dialect (R5RS/R7RS-compatible core, continuations, ratios, hash-tables, first-class environments, non-hygienic define-macro, no syntax-rules). It is a different language and API from Duktape or Lua, not a drop-in replacement.
how_it_is_fast: There is no bytecode compiler: s7 walks the list structure, but an optimizer annotates each expression in place with a specialised opcode and direct C function pointers (the fx_* and opt_info paths), so safe calls with constant, symbol or nested safe arguments skip the general eval loop and, in numeric code, can work on unboxed s7_int and s7_double values. Cells come from a pre-allocated heap of fixed-size cells popped off a free list and reclaimed by a mark-and-sweep GC. Current s7 also has pattern-specific recursion ops (for example OP_RECUR_IF_A_A_opLA_LAq) that run fib-shaped functions as native C recursion over unboxed integers; the 2015 copy that was benchmarked has none of these (no OP_RECUR code in the vendored s7.c).
when_to_use: A C or C++ application (especially audio or music software: Snd, Common Music, Scheme for Max/Pd, Radium all embed it) that wants Lisp/Scheme as its scripting layer and a two-file drop-in with no required dependencies.
Several isolated interpreters in one process: each s7_init instance is independent, and the docs show 16 instances running in 16 pthreads.
Numeric script code where you can register typed C fast paths (s7_set_d_dd_function and friends) so the optimizer calls them on unboxed doubles.
Replacing a 2015-era Duktape 1.x on call-heavy script code where a Lisp syntax is acceptable to your users.
when_not_to_use: Raw interpreter speed is the priority: in the same Scriptorium table PUC Lua (1.341 s), Chibi-Scheme (1.009 s) and LuaJIT with the JIT off (0.521 s) beat s7 (2.136 s) on fib(34).
Your users expect JavaScript or Lua, or you need syntax-rules / hygienic macros (s7 has only define-macro and says its macros are not hygienic).
Scheme-level threads sharing one heap: removed in 2011; one interpreter per thread only.
You need a reviewed, issue-tracked GitHub project: this repo is a 1-star, manually updated mirror; development, bug tracking and releases happen on CCRMA's cm-gitlab and in Snd tarballs.
Builds where compile time or binary size matter: s7.c is one roughly 3.8 MB C file (the source notes a 49-second compile in 2022).

integration.form: source-drop (s7.c + s7.h compiled into your program); optional WITH_MAIN standalone REPL
integration.dependencies: none (libm; optional gmp, mpfr and mpc with WITH_GMP; dlopen for WITH_C_LOADER)
integration.min_toolchain: C compiler with setjmp.h; the source says it no longer compiles with gcc 4.3 and that g++ 4.4 is too old; also compiles as C++ (HAVE_COMPLEX_TRIG 0) and with MSVC (both complex switches 0); exact minimum not documented
integration.platforms: Linux, macOS, FreeBSD/NetBSD/OpenBSD, Windows (MSVC, mingw, msys2), tcc, WebAssembly; 64-bit assumed by default (SIZEOF_VOID_P 4 for 32-bit)
integration.thread_safety: Each s7_scheme instance is independent and may run in its own thread; a single instance must not be shared between threads (Scheme-level threads were removed in August 2011).

gotchas: Harness limits behind the 4.5x: Scriptorium's bench.exe times five whole-process system() launches (start-up included) and never checks the printed result; s7 has a single bench.csv row (2.13558 s, s7 3.31 of 16-Jul-15 built with cl /Ox /Oy /MT /DNDEBUG /DWITH_MAIN) from a later session than Duktape's 9.544 s row, and the README keeps each engine's minimum across sessions. The test is one fib(34) micro-benchmark on Duktape 1.2.2, which is much older than Duktape 2.x.

The measured binary is eleven years older than the code you would vendor today: current s7 adds pattern-matched recursion ops that turn exactly this kind of if-shaped fib into native C recursion (s7.html claims fib(40) in 0.8 s, 'approximately the same as sbcl'), so a fib benchmark of current s7 would test a special case rather than general interpreter speed; whether the two-clause cond form in Scriptorium's tests/fib.scm hits those ops was not determined (the cond variant with two recursive calls in the source needs a four-element cond).

Errors longjmp out of s7 calls (s7_error unwinds the Scheme stack, then longjmps the C stack), so C++ frames between your entry point and a failing s7 call skip their destructors; values held in C across allocating calls must be protected with s7_gc_protect or the *_via_stack variants.

With MSVC (and tcc) HAVE_COMPLEX_NUMBERS is 0, and the docs warn that complex functions then become stubs that return their argument, so (sqrt -2) can return something bogus without an error; non-gmp builds use fixed 64-bit s7_int.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick s7 over Chibi-Scheme when you want a single-file drop-in with first-class environments, define-macro and typed C fast paths for numeric/DSP code, or the CCRMA audio ecosystem; pick Chibi (1.009 s vs 2.136 s on the same table, R7RS with syntax-rules) when standards conformance or interpreter speed matter more, and Lua or Luau when users expect a conventional scripting syntax.
verified_claims_summary: In r-lyeh's Scriptorium (July 2015, AMD A10 3.8 GHz, Windows 7 64-bit, MSVC VS2015 RC or VS2013, both engines built /Ox /Oy /MT /DNDEBUG), whole-process time for recursive fib(34), averaged over 5 launches, was 2.136 s for s7 3.31 versus 9.544 s for Duktape 1.2.2, about 4.5x (derived from page data; 4.2x to 4.5x against Duktape's other runs); PUC Lua at 1.341 s was about 1.6x faster than s7.
status_note: The upstream s7 is actively developed by its author at CCRMA (Snd 26.7 released 2026-09-07) and is 0BSD, so copyable, but this GitHub mirror stopped at s7 10.8 (17-Apr-2024) and the only speed evidence is one 2015 fib micro-benchmark of a version that predates most of the current optimizer.
